source.title: Balancing accuracy and efficiency in particle tracking: analyzing image resolution and batch size trade-offs
source.authors: H. Aghaei; R. Yazdanfar; Zahra Pouraskarparast; Qianjing Tang; E. Nikooee; Amir Raoof

record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects on held-out image-prediction error in particle tracking, an application outside the image-classification and language-model settings named in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper measures performance on unseen frame pairs and a blind holdout set, but does not measure training error or random-label fitting. Its findings bear on V5 as a batch-size extension; the other versions concern different behaviors or settings.
record.test_reason: The study compares held-out performance after training SimVP with batches 4 and 8 for the same 200 epochs. This tests V5's batch-size effect in a new setting, particle-frame prediction, although the verification comparison changes a tracking parameter alongside batch size.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: batch 4 gives better reported accuracy and perceptual metrics, including on unseen and blind data. They attribute this to more updates per epoch and beneficial gradient noise. Longer training closing the gap is an explanation drawn from prior work, not an intervention tested here.
record.recipe_differences: A batch-size comparison under a fixed 200-epoch budget, but in SimVP particle-frame prediction rather than classification or language modeling; batch 4 and batch 8 were also used at different resolutions in the primary sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Image resolution (64–400 px) and batch size (4 or 8) vary. The unseen-pair verification reports batch comparisons at 256, 300, and 400 px; the blind test is at 256 px.
record.problems: Only one architecture was examined. Batch-size comparisons used the same epoch count, but the authors note batch-8 runs received half as many parameter updates per epoch and may have been effectively undertrained. The paper does not report training-versus-test error gaps or random-label fitting.
record.rows_left_out: The table extraction is limited to MSE comparisons on unseen and blind evaluation sets, which directly test held-out performance. Other reported measures (MAE, RMSE, SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) were not extracted as separate rows because they add no conflicting direction to the MSE comparisons; primary-sweep resolution results do not supply matched batch comparisons across all resolutions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width changes beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.
Classification and language workloads; locating a batch-size threshold; longer training or matched update counts; interventions using learning-rate scaling, warmup, normalization, or regularization.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: The primary sweep contains a matched 300 × 300 batch comparison: MSE 0.695 for batch 8 versus 0.112 for batch 4. The explanation for omitted primary-sweep results obscures this available comparison. Record it separately, with evaluation-split provenance clarified.

record.verdict_notes: No original-source exclusion applies. Table 6 standard deviations describe variation across frame pairs, not independent training runs. Its batch-dependent tracking limits are a material omitted condition. The text also inconsistently describes convergence by 150 epochs and batch-8 undertraining; neither establishes the mechanism of the held-out difference.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.

Image-classification and language-model tasks; comparisons to longer training, learning-rate scaling with warmup, normalization or regularization changes; comparisons within the same epoch budget using other batch-adaptation recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training-test gap.

relationships.condition: Reported blind holdout performance of SimVP at 256 × 256 pixels after 200 epochs, batch 8 versus batch 4.
relationships.reason: r7–r8 report higher holdout MSE for batch 8: 0.525 versus 0.353. This supports the predicted direction in video prediction, subject to unspecified blind-test tracking settings.
relationships.display_finding: Holdout mean squared error (MSE) was 0.525 at batch 8 versus 0.353 at batch 4. The study did not explain how it monitored blind-test performance, so it is unclear whether batch size caused the difference.
